title: Kondañña sees
hook: whatever has the nature to arise has the nature to cease; Kondañña understands (SN 56.11)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dhammacakka, the first sermon: two extremes, a middle way, four truths, eight parts. The wheel turns.

Sometimes you hear a thing a hundred times and then, one day, you actually hear it. A song lyric. Something your grandmother used to say. It clicks, and you can't unhear it. The first sermon has just ended. Five men have heard the whole thing, the extremes, the truths, the path. Four of them are still turning it over. But one, a man named Kondañña, is sitting very still. Something in him has gone quiet and clear. The texts say the Buddha looks at him and says, out loud, with what sounds like joy: Kondañña has understood.
screen: `ONE DAY YOU ACTUALLY HEAR IT.` → `FIVE LISTENED. ONE SAW.` → `KONDAÑÑA HAS UNDERSTOOD.`

segments.voice: What Kondañña saw fits in one sentence. The sutta puts it like this: whatever has the nature to arise, all of that has the nature to cease. Anything that begins, ends. It sounds almost too plain to matter. But notice how rarely anyone lives as if they knew it. You grip a good mood as if it will stay, and brace against a bad one as if it will never leave. Kondañña didn't learn a new fact. He saw an old one all the way through, and the texts call that the opening of the eye of the dhamma, a clear, stainless eye. The Buddha is so glad that Kondañña gets a new name from that moment: Añña Kondañña, Kondañña who understood. And there's a lovely old thread here. Later tradition says Kondañña was one of the wise men called to look at the newborn prince, all those years ago in Kapilavatthu, and the only one who said with certainty that this boy would become a Buddha. If so, the first person to predict it became the first to understand it. Now look back at this week, the setting of the wheel. Seven weeks under the trees after the awakening, sheltered. Two merchants and the very first gift of food. The long question of whether to teach at all, and the answer that some are ready. Upaka on the road, not ready yet. The Deer Park, where five doubters stood up. The first sermon. And today, one man sees. The wheel has made its first turn.
screen: `WHATEVER ARISES, CEASES.` · `THE EYE OF THE DHAMMA OPENS.` · `KONDAÑÑA WHO UNDERSTOOD.` · `A WEEK OF THE WHEEL TURNING.` · then, large: `IT ARISES, IT ENDS.`

segments.voice: Pick one small thing and watch it from beginning to end: a breath is perfect, from the first cool touch at the nose, filling, turning, leaving, gone, and a new one arriving. Or follow a sound in the room, or an itch, from its first moment to its last. You're not holding on to anything; just watch it arise, and watch it end.
Kondañña sees. The first of the five to understand: whatever has the nature to arise has the nature to cease.
Your line: it arises, it ends. One man saw it, and came away with a new name. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhists remember Kondañña as the first disciple to understand the teaching, and the line 'whatever has the nature to arise has the nature to cease' is recited in the first sermon, which is chanted in many Theravada monasteries.

fork.setup: the sermon is over. one of your five listeners has clearly understood. what do you do?
options: say nothing, and wait for the others.
say aloud, with joy, that he has understood.
ask him to give the next sermon.
fork.reveal: the Buddha says it out loud: Kondañña has understood. and the name sticks: Añña Kondañña.

original.note: Pali: he has understood. The Buddha's words about Kondañña, which became part of his name.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old man nodding along at the end of a talk.
what it means: the first person to see the teaching for himself: whatever begins, ends.
what a scholar hears: yam kiñci samudayadhammam, sabbam tam nirodhadhammam, SN 56.11; the 'dhamma eye' marks what later tradition calls stream-entry.

sources.ref: Jataka Nidanakatha (the naming of the prince)

notes: The arising/ceasing formula is paraphrased from SN 56.11, not quoted from a named translation.

Kondañña as the youngest of the brahmins at the naming who alone predicted Buddhahood with certainty comes from the Jataka Nidanakatha (commentarial); the Nidanakatha makes him the youngest of the eight brahmins; the script says only 'later tradition says'. Confirm.
The 'dhamma eye' (dhammacakkhu) equated with stream-entry in the trapdoor, following commentarial usage; confirm.
